hints: Look at what happens to the carbon skeleton in each step, are atoms added across a bond, swapped, or removed?
In reaction 1 the C=C double bond in propene disappears as H and I both join the molecule to give one product.
In reaction 2 the I in $\text{CH}_3\text{CHICH}_3$ is swapped for OH from KOH to make the alcohol, with no double bond formed.
walkthrough:
**Classify Reaction 1**

Look at the starting alkene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$. It has a C=C double bond.

In reaction 1, $\text{HI}$ adds across that double bond:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{HI} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CHICH}_3$$
Two reactants become one product, and the double bond becomes a single bond. That is electrophilic addition.

**Classify Reaction 2**

Now start from the iodoalkane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHICH}_3$. It reacts with aqueous $\text{KOH}$.

The equation is:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CHICH}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3 + \text{I}^-$$
The I atom leaves and the OH group takes its place on the same carbon. One group swaps for another, so this is nucleophilic substitution.

**Put It Together**

Reaction 1 adds H-I across C=C, so addition. Reaction 2 swaps I for OH, so substitution.

That combination matches addition followed by substitution.

options.A: Reaction 1 is correctly addition, but reaction 2 is not elimination. Elimination would remove $\text{HI}$ to reform a C=C double bond, whereas here $\text{OH}$ replaces $\text{I}$ to give propan-2-ol.
options.B: Reaction 1 is addition because $\text{H}$ and $\text{I}$ add across the C=C of propene to form a single saturated product. Reaction 2 is substitution because $\text{I}$ is replaced by $\text{OH}$ from aqueous KOH to form the alcohol.
options.C: Reaction 1 is not elimination. Elimination starts from a saturated molecule and forms a double bond plus a small molecule, but here we start from an alkene and the double bond is lost as two atoms add.
options.D: Neither label fits in this order. Reaction 1 does not swap one atom for another on a saturated carbon, so it is not substitution. Reaction 2 does not create a double bond, so it is not elimination.
